new_head_para: So too the Romans and Carthaginians, worn out by their labors through the unbroken succession of dangers, were utterly past feeling, their strength sapped and their resolve undone by the long years of taxes and expenses. The Romans were fighting on with the same desperate spirit. For nearly five years now they had entirely withdrawn from operations at sea, both because of their reverses there and because they had become convinced they would decide the war by their land forces alone.
note: Greek is continuous (παρεῖντο … διὰ τὰς εἰσφορὰς); remove stray dashes at join.

new_head_para: His crews, with their fine physical condition, rode the swell with ease, and he quickly drew up his fleet in a single line, prow facing the enemy. The Carthaginians, seeing that the Romans were blocking their crossing, lowered their masts and, after each ship’s company had exhorted one another, closed with their opponents.
note: Greek continuous (ἀντίπρωρον κατέστησε τοῖς πολεμίοις); remove doubled dashes.

new_head_para: From this it is clear—as I proposed at the outset—that it was not by chance, as some of the Greeks suppose, nor by accident, but with very good reason that the Romans, having trained themselves in such great affairs, not only set their hands boldly to the rule and dominion of the whole world, but also achieved their purpose. And here one might naturally be puzzled as to the reason why, now that they have mastered the whole world and possess a superiority many times greater than before, they would be unable either to man so many ships or to put to sea with such great fleets as they once did.
note: Greek continuous (ἀλλὰ καὶ καθίκοντο τῆς προθέσεως); dash after 'but also' ungrammatical.

new_head_para: And all of them, recalling the promises their generals had made to encourage them in moments of crisis, conceived high hopes and great expectations of the redress that was coming to them. So, as soon as they had all assembled at Sicca, and Hanno—who was then the Carthaginian general in Libya—arrived and, far from fulfilling their hopes and the promises made to them, spoke instead of the weight of the tribute and the general financial straits of the city, and tried to get them to forgo even part of the wages acknowledged to be owed them, at once dissension and faction arose, and continual gatherings took place, sometimes by nationality, sometimes of them all together.
note: Greek has one phrase (τῆς ἐσομένης … ἐπανορθώσεως); English duplicated 'redress'; duplicate removed.
Greek runs on (περὶ τῶν ἀμφισβητουμένων); no gap.
Greek runs on (κατέστησαν αὑτῶν στρατηγοὺς Μάθω καὶ Σπένδιον); no gap.

new_head_para: And they themselves, more than anyone, had been the cause of such great evils. For during the previous war, supposing that they had reasonable grounds for it, they had governed the people of Libya with great harshness.
note: Greek has only τοιούτων καὶ τηλικούτων κακῶν (split); 'and of such grievous troubles' is a duplicate; removed.

new_head_para: Encamping at both of these points, the mercenaries had now cut the Carthaginians off from the countryside and went on to lay plans against the city itself, approaching the wall sometimes by day and sometimes by night, and throwing those inside into utter fear and confusion. As for Hanno, he was capable enough when it came to preparations, for he had a natural talent for this side of things; but once he set out with his army he was a different man, for he made poor use of his opportunities and handled affairs as a whole with inexperience and sluggishness.
note: Greek has one clause (ὁλοσχερεῖς ἐνέβαλλον τοὺς ἔνδον); 'they struck panic' duplicate removed. Paragraph tail beyond visible text must be kept as in file.
Greek runs on (ἐπὶ τοὺς τὴν γέφυραν φυλάττοντας); no gap.

new_head_para: And so the Carthaginians suddenly found the Libyans encamped in front of them, the Numidians at their rear, and Spendius’s men on their flank, which threw them into great difficulty and left them hard to escape. At this very time there was a man named Narávas, one of the most distinguished Numidians and full of warlike energy. He had always been well disposed toward the Carthaginians, having an inherited bond of friendship with them, and at this moment he was all the more spurred on by his admiration for Hamilcar the general.
note: Greek has one clause (μεγάλην ἀπορίαν περιστῆναι καὶ δυσέκφευκτον); English doubled it; merged.

new_head_para: Such, then, was the situation of the forces in the field. The Carthaginians, hemmed in on every side, were compelled to fall back on their hopes from the cities allied with them.
note: Greek: τὰ μὲν περὶ τὰς ὑπαίθρους δυνάμεις ἐν τούτοις ἦν — one clause; 'this was their state' duplicate.
